newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-STOJKO IS THE STALLONE OF THE ICE RINK.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-STOJKO IS THE STALLONE OF THE ICE RINK.

text.p: Elvis Stojko is the Sylvester Stallone of figure skating, a powerful performer who has a black belt in karate and lists dirt biking among his hobbies.
Compared with the classic artistry of skaters such as Russian Olympic champion Alexei Urmanov, Canada's Stojko has long been seen as the sport's action hero.

Early this month he became the only skater to land a quadruple-triple jump in competition, and while his technical ability won him back-to-back world titles in 1994 and 1995, he is still short of respect artistically.
Dressed all in black, complete with studded wrist bands, Stojko was talking tough as he once again defended his approach following the qualifying round at the world championships on Sunday.
"I have a harder, more powerful style but I still have the finesse," said Stojko. "I don't know what more they want, to be honest.
"The quality of movement is there, the motion is there. All the lines are there, the footwork is there, the jumps are there and the expression is there. What else?
"It almost feels like every time I do a programme, people feel there should be a little bit more -- but they never say what.
"I'm sticking with my game plan and sticking with the programme. I won't allow anyone to tell me what to do out there because then you're not an artist."
By Stojko's own admission, his artistic view of the sport might best be described as minimalist.
"If you do a lot of add-ons or more stuff, would that make it artistically better?" questioned Stojko. "No it doesn't."
It's easy to see how Stojko's artistic abilities are sometimes overlooked.

Stojko twisted his way into figure skating history in the Champions Series final in Hamilton, Ontario, when he became the first skater to land a quad-triple, a gravity-defying manoeuvre that requires four revolutions in the air followed immediately by three more - all in less than two seconds.
As Stojko's coach Doug Leigh likes to point out, more people have landed on the moon than have landed a quad-triple.
While Stojko's action-packed free skating, which also includes eight triples, two in combination, may not be winning over the critics, the 24-year-old Canadian is good box-office among the fans.
Talk before the championships did not centre on Urmanov's interpretative ability but when would Stojko launch another quad-triple.
Stojko left the opening day crowd holding it's breath in anticipation, but the combination foundered when he tumbled landing the quad, leaving him no opportunity to add the triple.
Stojko later explained that he never intended to attempt the combination. "I just wanted to have a nice setup for the quad.
"You just try to get the pattern, the setup and feel for it. It felt good so we're on track for Thursday.
"Doing the jump in practise is one thing, doing it in competition is a totally different matter.
"If you fall you have to hold the whole programme together after, so it's a different ball game."
